Extraordinary Shifts of the Leidenfrost Temperature from Multiscale Micro/Nanostructured Surfaces
top_cited_works.abstract: In the present work, the effects of surface chemistry and micro/nanostructuring on the Leidenfrost temperature are experimentally investigated. The functional surfaces were fabricated on a 304 stainless steel surface via femtosecond laser surface processing (FLSP). The droplet lifetime experimental method was employed to determine the Leidenfrost temperature for both machine-polished and textured surfaces. A precision dropper was used to control the droplet size to 4.2 μL and surface temperatures were measured by means of an embedded thermocouple. Extraordinary shifts in the Leidenfrost temperatures, as high as 175 °C relative to the polished surface, were observed with the laser-processed surfaces. These extraordinary shifts were attributed to nanoporosity, reduction in contact angle, intermittent liquid/solid contacts, and capillary wicking actions resulting from the presence of self-assembled nanoparticles formed on the surfaces. recent_works.title: A Concept of a Convection–Cloud Chamber to Study Aerosol–Cloud–Drizzle Interactions
recent_works.venue: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Understanding and quantifying the full chain of processes from aerosol activation to drizzle formation, and the associated feedbacks to the aerosol chemical and physical properties, all within a turbulent cloud are some of the toughest challenges in atmospheric chemistry and physics and are keys to the cloud–precipitation puzzle. This paper describes a concept for a new type of research facility consisting of a cloud chamber plus associated instrumentation and computational models, to explore aerosol–cloud interactions and processing, cloud optical properties, entrainment–cloud interactions, and quantitative assessment of drizzle onset. The envisioned design is for a 3 m × 3 m × 9 m chamber, such that the height is sufficient to achieve long lifetimes for aerosol processing and for significant drizzle growth by collision and coalescence. A suite of computational tools for simulating microphysical properties in the chamber provides a digital twin for designing the chamber and a range of example experiments. recent_works.title: A novel femtosecond laser surface processing system for functionalization of the inside of tubes with applications in enhanced thermal-fluid performance
recent_works.abstract: Roughening the inner surfaces of tubes is a widely used manufacturing approach to enhance heat transfer capabilities in both single-phase and two-phase flow regimes by increasing the effective surface area, increasing nucleation sites, improving wicking, and promoting turbulence and mixing. However, conventional fabrication techniques involve multistep, complex processes that are time-consuming, geometry limited, not easily scalable, and result in non-uniform structures. Here, we present a novel functional prototype, a single-step method for processing interior tube surfaces using self-organized laser functionalization (SOLF) with a high-power 300-watt femtosecond laser system (Amplitude Tangor 300). SOLF is a cutting-edge technique that produces self-organized permanent hierarchical micro- and nano-scale structures proven to significantly improve thermal-fluid performance. While past research with SOLF has focused predominantly on flat surfaces, many practical energy systems rely on tubular components, where SOLF implementation has been limited and understudied. recent_works.title: Toward increased throughput of femtosecond laser surface processed silicon: The effect of increased thermal loading on microstructure self-organization
recent_works.abstract: With increased transistor densities and the push to 3D chip architecture, thermal management in high power electronics has become an important and rapidly advancing area of research. One method for managing extreme heat fluxes generated by chip stacks is direct-to-chip two-phase heat transfer, where excess heat created by the high power electronics is used to force a change of state of a coolant from liquid to vapor. In the past, permanent, self-organized femtosecond laser-induced micro- and nano-scale surface features have shown to enhance the performance of two-phase heat transfer systems by enhancing the efficiency at which the surfaces boil, leading to decreases in device temperatures and overall power consumption, and limiting thermal strain on the devices. Previously, the industrial viability of the femtosecond laser surface processing (FLSP) methods was limited due to low throughput. However, the new generation of high repetition rate (>10 kHz), high pulse energy (>1 mJ) femtosecond lasers provide a path toward the integration of the FLSP of materials into industrialized devices. recent_works.title: Quasi‐Periodic Surface Functionalization by Ultra‐Short Pulsed Laser Processing: Unlocking Superior Heat Transfer in Vapor Chambers
recent_works.abstract: Abstract High‐power‐density modern electronics necessitate efficient and reliable heat removal at heat fluxes exceeding 1 kW cm − 2 , a demand that challenges the limits of conventional cooling strategies. The precise functionalization of surfaces is pivotal in developing advanced thermal management solutions for next‐gen electronics cooling. Herein, it is demonstrated for the first time that picosecond‐laser functionalization of copper surfaces—comprising densely packed, self‐organized, quasi‐periodic microstructures—results in surfaces that are highly suited for such applications. The methodology uses large laser beams (typical radius of 150µm or higher) to facilitate the self‐organization of laser‐formed surface features that are orders of magnitude smaller. recent_works.title: Femtosecond Laser Surface Processing (FLSP) of Silicon for Pool Boiling Enhancement Using Dielectric PF-5060
recent_works.abstract: Surface modification of silicon to improve pool boiling performance using PF-5060 as the working fluid was investigated. PF-5060, a dielectric fluid, is ideal for direct electronics cooling, however, its low critical heat flux (CHF) poses a significant limitation. To address this issue, femtosecond laser surface processing (FLSP) was employed to modify silicon surfaces. This manufacturing technique creates quasi-periodic microstructures with nanoscale surface roughness, thereby increasing the surface area available for heat transfer. These structures also provide an abundance of potential nucleation sites of varying sizes to further enhance two-phase heat transfer. Three FLSP silicon samples were created and evaluated in a pool boiling system up to CHF, with performance compared against a polished baseline. FLSP samples demonstrated consistent improvements in CHF, achieving a maximum enhancement of 24% with a peak value of $24.9 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$. Additionally, FLSP samples maintained lower surface temperatures across all heat flux levels compared to the baseline.
